rv.q: Designer Ti Green’s hospital is a gilded period piece – as poised as the medical knowledge of the period was unsteady, with not an antiseptic surface in sight. But it is for Rylance’s character study of the doctor that this show is a must-see (the medical history is of interest too).
Here in London it feels mighty, a show that uses every facet of theatricality, sometimes all at once.
But as a chance to witness Rylance's peculiar stage magic, this is a show not to be missed.
Rylance is one of this country’s very finest actors, but he should select his material more judiciously than this.
Dr Semmelweis is utterly fascinating in every respect, especially as it unearths such a vital piece of forgotten, or ignored, history.
It's an extraordinarily subtle and emotional performance.
You will leave Dr Semmelweis both proud of our species’ dedication to science and downtrodden by our hubristic stubbornness, our cruel capacity to silence those who challenge authority.

This new play, written by Stephen Brown with Rylance...is a perplexing animal – passionate, instructive, imaginatively directed, but also sometimes stilted and, at its heart, lacking the nuanced characterisation we have come to expect from its star.
Rylance, as ever, is magnetic, but even Morris’ production cannot disguise the fact that the actor has conceived a better role than a play.
Virtually everything in Tom Morris’s production lacks originality.

cn.t: Rylance delivers a magnetic, must-see performance as the tormented doctor, but the production's striking design and occasional dramatic moments can't fully compensate for a script that struggles to dramatize its important ideas.
